LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_PAGE_ECON_CRISES_EXPL: Crises in Exploration
LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_PAGE_ECON_CRISES_MODE: Crises in Modern
LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_PAGE_ECON_CRISES_OVER:
Economics gives every
            civilization an economy that can go wrong: the world's business cycle, the loans it carries, the prices it
            trades at, the inflation idle Gold suffers. A crisis is the moment one of those readings crosses a line.
            It isn't rolled and it isn't saved for the end of the age; the mod reads the state of your economy every
            turn, and a crisis can start on any turn of any age. While it lasts, the World tab shows what's pulling
            you down and what you can do about it.

Each response you take
            changes something at once, costs you something, and leaves a legacy you carry for a while or for the rest
            of the age. The history is the guide: the choices Solon, Philip II, Isaac Newton and Franklin Roosevelt
            made are the choices on the panel, with their prices and their aftermath.

A Depression comes when your
            own index on the World tab falls under 0.80. A credit panic comes in Exploration (from the Banking stage)
            and Modern when a Panic freezes the lenders while you hold loans, or when a bubble bursts. A price shock
            comes when the price of a resource class you import or export has moved 40 percent, up or down, on ten
            turns ago. A debt crisis comes after three turns with your payments due above your income, or when you
            default on a loan from another civilization. Runaway inflation (Exploration from Public debt, and
            Modern, with the Inflation option on) comes after five turns with the rate at its cap, or ten turns after
            you leave the gold standard. A trade collapse comes in Exploration and Modern when a third of your trade
            routes end within five turns.

A civilization has at most
            one crisis of a kind every 30 turns and two crises at once. A crisis ends the turn its condition stops
            holding, and the notice names what ended it: the responses you took, or the world recovering on its
            own.

While a crisis is open, the
            World tab of the Economics screen opens a Crisis section above the index. It names the crisis, the turn it
            began and the events behind it; it lists the responses standing and how long each has left; and it offers
            the responses open to you this age, each with what it does now, what it costs and what it leaves. A
            response goes through at the start of the next turn, like a loan request. You can end a standing response
            early from the same section, and some remember being cut short.
Doing nothing, and the Hoover trap

Doing nothing is a choice
            too. The world's index drifts back toward 1.00 by a tenth of the gap each turn, so a Depression left alone
            lifts in time, unless the cycle's momentum and new bad news hold it down. Meanwhile the slump charge takes
            a share of your income, the bond market's rates rise with the gap, and a Panic freezes the lenders: all
            of it leaning the wrong way, as it did in 1930.

Two responses make it
            worse, as they did then. Raising tariffs in a Depression (Smoot-Hawley's line) has the computer players
            answer in kind, and once three civilizations hold a High tariff while the world is under 0.80 the trade
            war pulls the index down by 0.005 a turn on its own. Austerity (Andrew Mellon's line) repays debt and
            mends your reputation while it pulls your own index down by 0.01 a turn. The panel marks both as the
            Hoover line so you take them with open eyes.

A legacy is the mark a
            response leaves after its immediate work is done: dearer loans for the age after a debasement, a credit
            cap that stays wider after lending to the crown, inflation that keeps running after leaving the gold
            standard. The Fiscal tab lists them under "What your choices left" with the turns each has left, or "for
            the age". Most clear at the age change; deposit insurance carries into the next age for a Market
            economy. A bank failure leaves a legacy on everyone at once.

A computer player in a crisis
            takes one response per crisis, chosen by its economic system (Economic systems in the Fiscal tab). A
            Planned or Manorial economy builds public works; a Mercantile one supports prices, charters a company or
            passes navigation acts, and is the one that will raise tariffs; a Religious one gives relief; a Tribute
            economy or a Palace economy levies tribute or turns to austerity; a Market or Corporatist economy insures
            its deposits and then builds. A civilization whose payments pass its income declares a bank holiday
            first, and one at war in Modern rearms. They pay the same prices and carry the same legacies you
            do.

"Crises and responses" is a
            setup option, on by default. Off, the business cycle runs as it does without the panel: a Depression is a
            phase you ride out, with the legacy cushion of your old buildings and the auto-loan guard for company, and
            nothing on this page applies.
LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_PAGE_ECON_CRISES_ANTI: The temple, the grain and the debt bondage

An ancient economy had few
            instruments and used them hard. Debt was personal and could cost a farmer his land or his freedom; the
            temple was the treasury and the first bank; grain was the price everyone watched; and the coin was the
            ruler's to make lighter. The Antiquity responses are those levers. A Depression here opens relief, public
            works and the bank holiday; a debt crisis opens the cancellation of debts, the temple's loan and, for a
            Tribute economy, a levy on its neighbours; a price shock opens the grain dole and the debased coin.
Cancel the debts

In 594 BC Athens handed
            Solon the power to settle a crisis in which smallholders had mortgaged their land and then themselves. His
            seisachtheia, the "shaking off of burdens", cancelled the debts secured on the person, freed those
            enslaved for debt and forbade the practice for good. Whether he also cancelled the debts on land, and
            whether he cut the coinage's weight as later writers claimed, is disputed; the freeing is not.

In the game it writes
            off every loan your citizens and the temple treasuries hold on you, lifts your own index by 0.02 and gives
            every settlement 4 Happiness a turn for five turns. The price: your credit reputation falls by 20, your
            citizens lend you nothing more this age, and the temple treasuries charge you half as much again for 20
            turns. Once per age, in a debt crisis or a Depression.
The grain dole

Rome's cura annonae
            began as Gaius Gracchus's subsidised grain in 123 BC and became, under Clodius in 58 BC, a free monthly
            ration for the citizens of the city. Emperors kept it for centuries because they didn't dare stop it: the
            dole was the price of a quiet capital, and a late fleet meant a riot.

In the game the dole is
            Antiquity's relief: 1 Gold a settlement a turn into the celebration meter, worth 4 Happiness a settlement,
            and a floor under this age's farm prices at nine tenths of what they were ten turns ago. It runs until the
            crisis ends and two turns beyond. End it early while the crisis is still on and the city remembers: 2
            Happiness off each settlement for ten turns.
Debase the coin

In AD 64 Nero cut the silver
            in the denarius and the weight of the aureus, and the coin that had held its standard since Augustus began
            a decline that later emperors carried to a few percent of silver. The mint could pay the army with the
            same bullion stretched further; the price of everything priced in denarii followed it up.

In the game you take three
            turns of your income out of the temple treasuries at once, and prices rise 2 percent a turn for five turns.
            The legacy is the Debased mark: every loan you take for the rest of the age costs a quarter more. Once
            per age, in a debt crisis, a Depression or a price shock.
Public works

Pericles put Athens to
            work on the Acropolis from 447 BC, the Parthenon first, paid largely from the treasury of the Delian League
            that Athens had moved to the city. Plutarch has his critics calling it dressing the city like a vain
            woman, and Pericles answering that the work fed every trade in Athens.

In the game public works
            spends 2 Gold a settlement a turn in Antiquity (4 in Exploration, 8 in Modern) straight into your
            settlements' current builds, at the game's own purchase rate, through the same account a development loan
            uses. While it runs your own index gains 0.01 a turn, and while the world is under 0.95 each civilization
            building adds 0.0025 to the world's, up to 0.01 a turn in all: stimulus pulls toward Steady and stops
            there. It runs until the crisis ends and three turns beyond; the builds are what it leaves.
Tribute

The Persian kings ran an
            empire on tribute. Herodotus lists what each of Darius's satrapies owed in talents of silver, and the
            reliefs at Persepolis show the delegations carrying it in. A king short of silver didn't borrow; he
            assessed.

In the game only a Tribute
            economy (Despotism) can levy. Each civilization Unfriendly or worse with you that you're stronger than
            pays you two turns of its income at once, from what it holds, and books 10 grievances against you. Once
            per crisis; the grudge is the legacy, and it lasts ten turns on the Fiscal tab's list.
The temple lends

Temples were the first
            banks. The Eanna at Uruk and the temple of Shamash at Sippar lent grain and silver at interest in the
            third and second millennia BC; the Parthenon's treasury lent Athens the money for the Peloponnesian War
            and kept the account on stone. A temple loan was a loan from the city's own reserve, taken when nobody else
            would lend.

In the game the temple
            treasuries open you a loan of three turns of your income over 20 turns at the age's base rate, outside
            your credit cap. The legacy falls on everyone: the temple treasuries charge a quarter more, for every
            civilization, for the rest of the age. Once per age, in a debt crisis or a Depression.
Bank holiday

The ancient form was a
            moratorium: a ruler's decree that debts stood still for a season. In the game it's the same response in
            every age. For three turns no payment on your loans falls due or counts as missed, nobody who owes you
            pays either, and your escrow holds; your own index gains 0.02 once for the breathing space. Each lender's
            relationship with you slips by 2 and your reputation by 3. Once per crisis.
Confidence

A ruler who speaks to the
            city steadies it. In the game, 20 Influence buys 0.01 on your own index, once every five turns, in any
            crisis of any age. It's the cheapest response and the smallest.
Austerity

Austerity is open in every
            age and is the same in each: while it runs you put half of whatever you hold above your reserve into your
            dearest loan each turn, your reputation gains 3 once, and your own index loses 0.01 a turn. It's the right
            answer when your trouble is debt and the wrong one when it's demand; the panel says which your figures
            look like. It runs until the crisis ends.
LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_PAGE_ECON_CRISES_EXPL: The bankers, the bullion and the companies

Between the Medici and the
            Bank of England the instruments multiplied: bankers who lent to kings, kings who defaulted on them, mints
            that recoined, chartered companies that traded with an army, navigation acts that kept the trade at home,
            and fleets of silver that raised every price in Europe. The Exploration responses are those, and the
            crises they answer come more often: a Panic can freeze the lenders from the Banking stage, inflation runs
            from Public debt, and a trade collapse can follow a war or a tariff.
Suspend payments

In 1557 Philip II of Spain
            suspended payment on his debts, the first of four such decrees in his reign, and turned his short-term
            loans into long bonds by fiat. The Fuggers of Augsburg, who had financed his father's election as
            emperor, were never fully repaid; Genoese bankers took their place and were caught by the next
            suspension in turn.

In the game it's a bank
            holiday on every loan you owe, three turns long, and the lenders remember it. Each civilization you owe
            loses 3 relationship and books 10 grievances, every one of them refuses to lend to you again this age,
            and the bond market charges you half as much again for 20 turns. Once per age, in a debt crisis, a credit
            panic or a Depression. Two suspensions in the world within five turns start a bankruptcy cascade (see
            the events page).
Recoinage

By 1695 England's silver
            coin had been clipped to about half its lawful weight and the exchange was in disorder. The Great
            Recoinage of 1696 called it all in and struck it anew at full weight, at a cost to the Treasury of some
            two and a half million pounds, with Isaac Newton at the Mint seeing the new coin through and prosecuting
            the clippers.

In the game it costs two
            turns of your income, paid into the inflation account, and clears the inflation your own choices added
            (a debased coin, bullion fleets, the gold standard left). The legacy is Steadied: erosion can take at most
            half of what it otherwise would from your idle Gold for the rest of the age. Needs Public debt; once per
            age, in runaway inflation or a price shock.
Charter a company

Elizabeth I chartered the
            East India Company on the last day of 1600, with a monopoly of English trade east of the Cape; the Dutch
            VOC followed in 1602 as the first company to sell shares to the public. Both paid dividends to their
            shareholders for two centuries, and both ended up ruling the places they had been chartered to trade
            with.

In the game, for 20 turns
            your credit cap gains two turns of income and your trade bills fall by a fifth. The company can't be
            closed: for the rest of the age a fifth of your route income goes to its shareholders, your citizens.
            Needs the Chartered companies stage and a trade route; once per age, in a trade collapse, a Depression or
            a debt crisis.
Navigation acts

England's Navigation
            Act of 1651 and its successors kept colonial trade in English ships and routed it through English ports:
            mercantilism as law. They fed three wars with the Dutch, who had carried that trade, and were repealed
            only in 1849.

In the game it sets
            your tariff to High for ten turns without the relationship cost a High tariff usually carries, and the
            civilizations you import from can't answer it in kind while it stands, since the acts are law. The legacy
            is the Hoover line's: for the rest of the age you count double toward a trade war. Needs the Tariffs
            stage; once per age, in a trade collapse, a price shock or a Depression.
Bullion fleets

From the 1540s the silver
            of Potosí and Zacatecas crossed the Atlantic in convoys, and Spain spent it. Prices in Spain and then
            across Europe rose for a century, the "price revolution"; how much of that was the silver and how much
            population growth is still argued, but the crown's income rose with the fleets and its wars rose
            faster.

In the game a fleet lands
            three turns of your income at once, and prices rise 3 percent a turn for five turns. The legacies: your
            own inflation runs 0.25 percent a turn faster for ten turns, and for 20 turns the pirates are out, so a
            trade collapse comes at half the loss of routes it otherwise takes. Once per age, in a debt crisis, a
            Depression or a credit panic.
Lend to the crown

The Medici bank lent to
            popes and kings and lived on it; the Fuggers lent Charles V the money that bought the imperial election
            of 1519 and took the Habsburg silver mines as security. A banker that deep in a crown's affairs couldn't
            let it fail without failing too.

In the game it needs a
            civilization Friendly with you that holds Gold. Your credit cap gains four turns of income for the rest of
            the age, as its lenders extend themselves on your account. Once per age, in a debt crisis, a credit panic
            or a Depression.
Public works

Thomas Gresham built the
            Royal Exchange in 1565 at his own expense and the Crown took it over; the canal age that began with the
            Bridgewater in 1761 was dug on borrowed money and paid for itself in coal. In the game public works in
            Exploration spends 4 Gold a settlement a turn into your builds, with the same 0.01 a turn on your own
            index and the same world share under 0.95 as in Antiquity. It runs until the crisis ends and three turns
            beyond.
Relief

The English Poor Laws of 1601
            made each parish responsible for its own poor and taxed it to pay for them. In the game relief is 1 Gold a
            settlement a turn into the celebration meter, worth 4 Happiness a settlement, until the crisis ends and
            two turns beyond; Emigration and Partisans read it as Happiness. Ending it early while the crisis is on
            costs 2 Happiness a settlement for ten turns.
Bank holiday

Three turns with no
            payment due or missed on your loans and none owed to you; 0.02 on your own index once; 2 relationship with
            each lender and 3 reputation. Once per crisis, as in every age. Suspending payments is the harder version,
            above.
Confidence

20 Influence for 0.01 on
            your own index, once every five turns, in any crisis.
Austerity

Half of what you hold above
            your reserve into your dearest loan each turn, 3 reputation once, and 0.01 a turn off your own index while
            it runs. The Hoover line in any age.
LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_PAGE_ECON_CRISES_MODE: The New Deal

The Great Depression began with
            the crash of October 1929 and ran, in the United States, to the war. Between 1929 and 1933 output fell by
            about a third, a quarter of the workforce was out of work, and some nine thousand banks failed. Herbert
            Hoover's administration raised tariffs, balanced budgets and waited; Franklin Roosevelt's first hundred
            days, from March 1933, tried most of what is on this page at once. The Modern responses are the New Deal,
            with the Hoover line kept on the panel so you can see what it cost.
Bank holiday

Roosevelt closed every bank
            in the country on 6 March 1933, two days after his inauguration, and the Emergency Banking Act of 9 March
            let the sound ones reopen under licence. Deposits flowed back in the week after, which is the whole point
            of a holiday: it stops the run long enough for confidence to return.

In the game, for three turns
            no payment on your loans falls due or counts as missed and nobody who owes you pays; your escrow holds and
            your own index gains 0.02 once. Each lender's relationship with you slips by 2 and your reputation by 3.
            Once per crisis.
Deposit insurance

The Banking Act of 1933,
            Glass-Steagall, created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and parted commercial banking from
            securities. Insured deposits ended the bank run as an American institution: with the government standing
            behind the account there was no longer a reason to be first in the queue.

In the game it costs
            two turns of your income, paid into the bond market as the fund, and lasts the age (a Market economy
            carries it into the next). While it stands a Panic hits your own index half as hard and the freeze on
            lenders doesn't apply to you, the bond market's spread never rises above 1.0 for you, and a bank run can't
            happen to you; the price is a credit cap whose depth term is cut by a quarter, since insured banks lend
            less. Needs the Banking stage; once in the game, in a credit panic, a Depression or a debt crisis.
Off the gold standard

In April 1933 the United
            States stopped paying out gold and called in the gold coin, and in January 1934 the dollar was fixed again
            at 35 dollars an ounce, down from 20.67: a devaluation of 41 percent. Britain had left gold in September
            1931. The countries that left first recovered first; the ones that stayed on it, France among them,
            stayed down longest.

In the game every loan
            you owe the bond market and the temple treasuries loses a tenth of what's outstanding, prices rise 3
            percent a turn for five turns, your inflation runs 0.5 percent a turn faster for those five turns and then
            0.25 percent faster for the rest of the age, and your own index gains 0.01 a turn for five turns. Each
            civilization you owe loses 3 relationship and books 10 grievances, and your reputation falls by 10. A
            Planned economy has no money to float. Needs Public debt; once per age, in a Depression, a debt crisis or
            a credit panic. Ten turns off gold opens a runaway-inflation crisis; a recoinage answers it.
Public works

The Civilian Conservation
            Corps put young men to work in the forests from 1933; the Tennessee Valley Authority dammed a river
            system; the Works Progress Administration of 1935 employed more than eight million people over its life
            building roads, schools, airports and bridges, and paid writers and painters too. Deficit spending as a
            cure for a slump had its theory in Keynes's General Theory of 1936, but the works came first.

In the game public works in
            Modern spends 8 Gold a settlement a turn into your settlements' current builds through the progress
            account, with 0.01 a turn on your own index and, while the world is under 0.95, 0.0025 on the world's for
            each civilization building, up to 0.01 a turn in all. A civilization in a Depression may borrow for it
            from the bond market even during a Panic: deficit spending, in the open. It runs until the crisis ends and
            three turns beyond; the builds stay.
Relief

The Federal Emergency Relief
            Administration of 1933 sent money to the states for direct relief, Britain's dole had carried its
            unemployed since 1911, and the Social Security Act of 1935 made the relief of old age permanent. In the
            game relief is 1 Gold a settlement a turn into the celebration meter, 4 Happiness a settlement, until the
            crisis ends and two turns beyond; the Emigration and Partisans mods read it as Happiness. End it early
            while the crisis is on and each settlement loses 2 Happiness a turn for ten turns.
Price supports

The Agricultural
            Adjustment Act of 1933 paid farmers to grow less so that prices would rise, and the National Recovery
            Administration's codes set prices and wages across industry until the Supreme Court struck the NRA down in
            1935. Farm prices did recover; whether the codes helped or held recovery back is still argued.

In the game it puts a
            floor under this age's farm (Bonus) resource prices at nine tenths of what they were ten turns ago, for
            everyone, and you pay for it: half your income a turn into the cycle account while it runs. It runs until
            the crisis ends. The legacy, for ten turns, is dearer imports for your partners: each civilization that
            imports from you loses 1 relationship every five turns. Once per crisis, in a price shock, a Depression or
            a trade collapse.
Rearmament

In the game, for ten turns
            your own index gains 0.005 a turn and a computer player's army budget runs at one and a half times its
            usual weight. The legacy is the army itself and what your neighbours' agendas make of it, on the list for
            20 turns. Once per age, in a Depression, a trade collapse or a credit panic.
Confidence

Roosevelt's first fireside
            chat, on 12 March 1933, explained the bank holiday to the country in plain words, and the banks reopened
            the next morning to queues of depositors putting money back. In the game, 20 Influence buys 0.01 on your
            own index, once every five turns, in any crisis.
The Hoover trap

The Smoot-Hawley Tariff of June
            1930 raised duties on some twenty thousand goods over the objection of a thousand economists; America's
            partners answered in kind, and world trade fell by about two thirds between 1929 and 1934. Andrew Mellon,
            Hoover's Treasury Secretary, is remembered for the advice to "liquidate labor, liquidate stocks,
            liquidate the farmers"; whether he said it is Hoover's word, but the policy of balanced budgets in a
            slump was real, and when Roosevelt tried it himself in 1937 the recovery stalled for a year.

In the game both are on the panel,
            marked. A High tariff in a Depression is answered in kind two turns later by every computer player you
            bill, each route that ends weighs 0.005 on the index, and once three civilizations hold High while the
            world is under 0.80 the trade war takes 0.005 more a turn from everyone. Austerity repays debt with half
            your surplus each turn and gains you 3 reputation, and takes 0.01 a turn from your own index while it
            runs. The panel tells you whether your figures look like a debt problem or a demand problem before you
            choose.
LOC_PEDIA_CONCEPTS_PAGE_ECON_CRISES_EVEN: Read from the state, not rolled

Nothing on this page comes from a
            dice roll. Each event is a reading the mod takes every turn from the ledger, the cycle and the map, and each
            one has a history behind it. They make a crisis worse, or mark its end.

The Bank of United States in
            New York failed in December 1930 with four hundred thousand depositors, the largest bank failure in the
            country's history to that day, and the runs spread from bank to bank through 1931 and 1932. A bank fails
            when enough of what it lent out goes bad at once and its depositors notice.

In the game a civilization in a
            Depression with two or more borrowers in default to it takes a run: its own index loses 0.02 once and it
            lends to nobody for five turns. Once per Depression. Deposit insurance stops it.

Some nine thousand American
            banks failed between 1930 and 1933, and with them the deposits of their customers and the lending of the
            rest, which is how a run becomes a depression. In the game, when the loans in default pass a fifth of all
            the world's loans while the world is in a Depression, the bond market closes for five turns to every
            civilization without deposit insurance, and every credit cap in the world loses two turns of income for
            the rest of the age. Once per age.

Drought on the ploughed-up
            plains from 1930 lifted the topsoil into storms that reached the Atlantic, and a farm economy already in a
            depression lost its land and its people to the roads. In the game a flood, eruption or storm on the land
            of a civilization in Depression weighs twice on the index: the disaster's usual weight, and the Dust Bowl's
            again.

In the summer of 1932 some
            forty thousand veterans of the Great War and their families camped in Washington to ask for the bonus
            they'd been promised for 1945, and in July the army cleared them out with cavalry, tanks and tear gas. A
            government that gives its people nothing in a depression hears from them. In the game a civilization five
            turns into a Depression with neither relief nor public works running loses 0.01 a turn on its own index
            until it starts one.

Tulips in 1637, the South Sea
            Company in 1720, stocks bought on margin in 1929: a boom in which credit grows faster than the thing it's
            buying, until the turn. In the game, when the world has read "credit growing fast" five turns running with
            the index above 1.05, the notice says a bubble is on. If the index then falls under 0.95 within ten turns,
            it bursts: a credit panic opens for every civilization holding loans, in the ages that have one. A bubble
            that deflates slowly instead is forgotten.

When Philip II suspended
            payment, the bankers who had lent to him couldn't pay the ones who had lent to them, and the stoppage ran
            through Antwerp and Augsburg. In the game two suspensions of payments in the world within five turns close
            the bond market to every civilization without deposit insurance for five turns.

A crisis ends the turn its
            condition stops holding. The notice names what ended it, the responses you took during it or the world
            recovering on its own, and the chronicle on the Treasury tab keeps the line. The responses that ran "until
            the crisis ends" wind down over their last few turns, and the legacies stay for as long as each says on
            the Fiscal tab.
